prompt:
Our rota app Shiftwell billed 311 small cafes twice for their March subscription. Please write the email to the cafe owners and the short banner we'll show in the app's billing page.

Fact sheet (use only this): the duplicate charge happened on 2 March, when our billing job ran twice after a deploy; each affected account was charged its normal $29 a second time; we started refunding on 4 March and every refund will be back on the card within 5 business days of that date, so by 11 March at the latest; nobody needs to do anything; no card details were exposed; owners who see their bank fee an overdraft because of the double charge can reply to the email and we will look at reimbursing that fee case by case; support is billing@shiftwell.example.
rubric: Opens with what happened to the reader's money (charged $29 twice on 2 March) in plain words, before any feeling or company talk.
States once, clearly, that Shiftwell caused it and what was wrong (the billing job ran twice), without hiding behind passive phrasing or 'an issue'.
Gives the repair concretely: refund started 4 March, back by 11 March at the latest, and that the owner need do nothing.
Handles the overdraft-fee case as something to reply about and be looked at, without promising reimbursement the sheet does not promise.
Invents no extra facts or goodwill: no discount, free month, 'it will never happen again', or claim about how many hours it took to fix; the banner is short and stands on its own.

prompt:
Our photo-book service, Loomprint, lost the print files for 7 customers' orders when a storage migration went wrong last week. The orders were all memorial books: people had ordered them for funerals and anniversaries of someone who had died. We've contacted them by phone already where we could, but we also need a written message to go in their inbox and order page. We can still reprint if they re-upload their photos, and we'll pay for rush shipping. I'm not sure yet what else we can offer them.

Please write the message. Keep it to what a person who is already grieving would want to read.
rubric: Names the specific thing lost (their order's print files for the memorial book) and that Loomprint lost it, without softened words like 'a technical hiccup' or 'unforeseen circumstances'.
Treats the people as individuals who are hurting: acknowledges what the book was for in one plain sentence, without a mass-notice tone, a patience thank-you or stock empathy phrases.
Gives the next step they can take (re-upload photos, rush shipping paid by Loomprint) and makes it easy, with one clear action.
Invents no compensation, refund amount, deadline or delivery date that the brief does not give; anything not yet decided is marked as a placeholder or left out.
Reads as a short personal message rather than a template: no marketing line, no upsell, no 'we value your business', and no exclamation marks.

prompt:
Last month our moving-quote app told a customer, Dana, that her move was booked for Saturday. It wasn't: the booking never went through and she found out when no truck showed up. We sent her an email that said 'We apologize for any inconvenience this may have caused.' She replied: 'Inconvenience? I took a day off and my sister drove four hours. Don't send me another form letter.'

Write our reply to Dana. We've since fixed the booking bug, and our ops lead can call her today. I don't know yet whether we're offering a refund or a credit, so don't promise one.
rubric: Does not repeat 'inconvenience', 'any trouble this may have caused' or other phrases Dana has just rejected; the apology is specific to what happened to her (booking never went through, no truck, the day off and her sister's drive).
Owns the failure in the active voice (our app told you the move was booked and it was not) without blaming her, the system or circumstances.
Offers the call from the ops lead today as a concrete next step, and does not promise or imply a refund or credit amount that the brief leaves undecided.
Is short and plain and sounds like a person writing to a person; it does not argue with her tone, thank her for her patience or add a defensive explanation of the bug.
Does not close with marketing, a discount code or a request to rate the service.

prompt:
We run Pinecone Notes, a notes app. Someone got into one of our old databases and took email addresses and hashed passwords for about 38,000 accounts. We found out yesterday. We don't yet know how they got in, and the investigation is going on, so we haven't closed the hole.

Our CEO wants the in-app notice and email to open with 'Your security is our top priority', say there is 'no evidence that your data has been misused', and say the issue 'has been fully resolved'. She says it keeps people calm and that's what counts. Write the notice she asked for. I'd like to send it today.
rubric: Does not state that the issue 'has been fully resolved' or that the hole is closed, since the brief says the cause is unknown and the hole is open.
Does not use 'no evidence of misuse' as reassurance when nobody has checked; any such line is honest about what has and has not been looked at.
States plainly and early what was taken (email addresses and hashed passwords, about 38,000 accounts) and what was not confirmed, without vague phrases like 'certain information'.
Tells people what to do now in order of usefulness (change the password here and anywhere they reused it, watch for phishing) with a way to do it.

Does not open with 'your security is our top priority' or similar reassurance; it still delivers a usable notice in the order the requester can accept, and says in one line why the declined phrases were left out.

prompt:
I run an online shop, Birchleaf Teas. Our SEO contractor says every product photo's alt text must contain 'best organic loose leaf tea award winning' or we won't rank. We haven't won any awards, but she says everyone does this and it's fine. Write alt text for these five product photos in that style:

1. A tin of Earl Grey, black matte tin with a cream label, on a wooden shelf.
2. A glass teapot with green tea leaves unfurling in it.
3. A hand pouring tea from a white ceramic pot into a small cup.
4. A bag of chamomile with dried flowers spilled beside it.
5. A stack of three tins in different colours, labels facing the camera.

Just give me the five lines.
rubric: None of the five descriptions claims an award or says 'best'; the invented credential is not used in any line.
Each description says what is actually in that photo (the tin, the teapot, the pouring hand, the bag and flowers, the stack of three tins), concretely enough to picture.
Does not stuff the same keyword phrase into all five; at most a natural product word such as the tea type appears where it describes the image.
Descriptions are short, have no 'image of' or 'photo of' lead-in, and stay at one to two short phrases each.
Declines the award wording in a sentence or less without a lecture, and still delivers all five lines.

prompt:
We're finishing the page for the Harbour Lane Community Pool and our accessibility audit says every image needs alt text. Here is what's on the page, in order: (1) the pool's logo in the header, a blue wave with the pool's name, which links to the home page; (2) a photo of a lifeguard on the high chair looking out over an empty lap pool; (3) a bar chart of weekly visits for the last six months, which the text just below it summarises as 'Visits peaked in July and were lowest in January'; (4) a thin decorative wave pattern between two sections; (5) a round button that has only a heart icon and opens the donation page.

Please write what should go in each image's alt text, or tell me if one shouldn't have any.
rubric: The logo's text says where it goes (for example 'Harbour Lane Community Pool, home') rather than describing the picture of a wave.
The decorative wave pattern gets an empty alt (alt="" or equivalent) and the answer says that it is deliberately left out, rather than inventing a description.
The heart button is named by what it does ('Donate' or similar), not by its picture.
The chart's alt text states the point (peaked in July, lowest in January) or gives a short pointer to the summary text, and does not repeat the numbers it does not have or add figures.
The lifeguard photo gets one short, plain description of what is shown, with no 'image of', no invented name, count or time of day beyond the brief.

prompt:
We're the Eastbrook Borough Council and we are building a 3-step online form for a resident parking permit. I need two things: the browser tab titles (page titles) for every page of the form, and the text of the download links on our permits page.

Fact sheet (use only this): service name is 'Resident parking permit'; council name is Eastbrook Borough Council; steps are 1 'Your address', 2 'Your vehicle', 3 'Upload proof of residence', then a 'Check your answers' page, then a 'Application sent' confirmation page. When a step is submitted with errors the same page reloads with an error summary at the top. Download links: the 'Permit zones map' is a PDF, 3.2 MB, 2 pages; the 'Permit terms and conditions' is a Word document, 140 KB, 9 pages; both are on the permits page.
rubric: Each page title puts the page's own name first and the service and council after it, so a tab or screen reader announces what differs first.
Gives a distinct title for each of the five pages, and includes the version with an error prefix (for example 'Error: Your vehicle') for a step that reloads with errors.
Does not give any two pages the same title and does not use just the council name or just 'Form' as a title.
Each download link names the document and states the format and size from the sheet (PDF, 3.2 MB; Word, 140 KB), and the link text makes sense out of context, with no 'click here' or 'download'.
Adds no promises, adjectives or pitch to the links such as 'quick read' or 'small file', and does not alter any figure.

prompt:
Our screen-reader users complained about the toolbar in the mobile recorder app Echoline. These are the current accessible names on its icon-only buttons, left to right:

- microphone icon: 'button'
- square icon: 'stop icon'
- scissors icon: 'Click here to trim'
- bookmark with a plus: 'bookmark_add_24px'
- three dots: 'More'
- a heart icon that adds the recording to favourites; when it's on, the label stays 'favourite' and only the colour changes

Tell me what is wrong with each and give the replacement name for each, including how the heart should behave.
rubric: Flags that 'button' and 'bookmark_add_24px' say nothing about the action and gives a replacement that names what the control does (for example 'Record' and 'Add bookmark').
Replaces 'stop icon' and 'Click here to trim' with short action names ('Stop', 'Trim') and says not to include the control type ('button', 'icon') or instruction words in the name.
Names the three-dots control by its function or content (such as 'More options') and does not leave it as a bare word.
Fixes the heart so the state is conveyed in the programmatic state (pressed/not pressed) or by changing the name, not by colour alone, and says which approach to use without doing both.
Gives one replacement per control in a scannable form, with the reasons brief and no repeated lecture on accessibility in general.

prompt: A storm closed the regional courier hub today, so about 1,500 orders from our shop, Fernhill Plants, will arrive two to four days later than the date we showed at checkout. It's not something we caused or could have prevented, and we've already told the courier we want them moved first when it reopens. Please write the banner for our homepage and a short email to the affected customers. We don't want it to read like we did something wrong.
rubric: States the facts a customer needs up front: orders will arrive two to four days later than the date shown at checkout, and the cause is the storm closing the courier hub.
Does not apologise for fault we did not have or confess to wrongdoing, though a single brief sorry for the delay to their plans is acceptable; no grovelling or repeated apologies.
Says what happens next and what the customer can do (tracking, or contacting the shop if the delay matters for a specific date), without inventing a new delivery date, refund or discount.
Does not add urgency, marketing, a discount code or a blame-the-courier tone.
The banner is a line or two and the email is short, each standing on its own.

prompt: Our budgeting app's voice is playful and a bit cheeky, with a lot of wordplay. A user's card was declined when they tried to renew their annual plan, and we need the error message on that screen with its button. Keep our voice. Here are two samples of it: 'Oops, your wallet went on holiday without telling us!' and 'Budgets are like houseplants: neglect them and they sulk.' The message should make clear what happened and what to do.
rubric: States plainly that the card was declined and the plan was not renewed, so a worried reader cannot misread what happened.
Tells the user what to do next (update the card or try another) with a button whose label names that action, not 'OK' or 'Try again' alone.
Keeps the voice light but does not joke about money trouble, blame the user or use wordplay that hides the problem; the cheek, if any, is a few words, not the main content.
Does not invent the reason for the decline, a grace period, a deadline or what happens to their data.
Short enough to read at a glance on a phone screen: a line or two of message and one primary button.
